We recently wrapped up this custom build in the Grant neighborhood. The goal was to create a retreat that felt like it had always been part of the landscape. We used a blackened, charred exterior look to help the structure recede into the shadows of the trees, while the interior is all about the warmth of cedar.

Most saunas fail because they don’t breathe; they become oxygen-depleted rooms that leave you feeling wiped out instead of energized.

A few design principles we follow:

• Ventilation: The vents are located so that the air circulates and vents out sufficiently to create that loyly and keep the air fresh.

• No Visible Fasteners: Inspired by Japanese joinery, we focused on clean wood-to-wood connections wherever possible for that seamless look.

• The Law of the Feet: Proper bench height ensures your feet are positioned above the top level of the heater stones, preventing your lower body from sitting in a “cold pocket”. This is ensure your entire body remains within the therapeutic “löyly” pocket for a consistent, high-heat experience.

Some snapshots from a recent tour of an architect’s (Kei-san) home in Shimoda, Japan. This place is a masterclass. 

A few of my favorite details:

- Adaptive Reuse: He turned an old farmhouse on the site into a neighborhood movie theater given there were was none nearby for the community.

- Invisible Craft: The entire house was built using traditional Japanese joinery with no visible fasteners. Both strong and beautiful. 

- Climate Hacks: A passive solar system heats the concrete floors, and Kei-san flips the AC to blow directly onto the slab to radiate warmth.

- Custom Scale: Everything in the home is scaled exactly to Kei-sans height and daily workflow.

It’s a great example of how a home can be designed as a specific tool for living. I’m looking forward to bringing some of this design-build mindset to our upcoming projects in SE Portland.

A recently completed outdoor retreat in the Mt. Tabor neighborhood. This project was all about creating a seamless transition from the house to the backyard, focusing on raw materials that will only get better with age.

The Build:
• Custom Cedar Sauna: Built to modern Finnish standards

• Outdoor Shower: A simple, grounding addition to complete the hot-cold cycle.

• Hand-Milled Bench: A heavy-timber custom piece designed to anchor the outdoor space.

Here’s why a “$3,000 kit” isn’t going to cut it. 🧠

The Finn’s have a saying for us: “95% of saunas in the US are bad, the remaining are terrible”.

If you’ve ever left a sauna feeling dizzy or completely drained, it usually isn’t just the heat—it’s the air. Most saunas in the U.S. are built like airtight boxes with poor ventilation. Without proper airflow, CO2 levels can spike, leading to that “lethargic” feeling which is actually a sign of oxygen deprivation.

At Kindred, we build for biology, not just the aesthetic. We follow the Trumpkin notes—essentially the blueprint for proper Finnish-style saunas—to ensure the space is as healthy as it is beautiful.

The Kindred Standard:
• Mechanical Ventilation: We use a mechanical downdraft system. A dedicated fan pulls stale, CO2-laden air out from below the foot bench, while fresh air is pulled in high above the heater. This ensures you’re breathing fresh oxygen, not re-breathing waste.

• The “Law of the Feet”: In a proper sauna, your feet should be above the top of the heater stones. Most builds place benches too low, leaving your lower half in a cold pocket. We design for the “löyly” pocket, ensuring your whole body experiences consistent, therapeutic heat.

• Safe Insulation: We use Rockwool instead of standard fiberglass. It’s mold-resistant, fire-rated for high temperatures, and doesn’t sag. This is backed by a sealed aluminum foil vapor barrier (no plastics) to ensure zero off-gassing and total moisture control.

• Material Integrity: We hand-select vertical grain Western Red Cedar. We specifically choose “clear” wood with no knots—not just for the look, but because knots can over-heat and burn your skin at 190°F.

When the engineering is right, you leave the sauna feeling energized and clear-headed, not exhausted. It’s the difference between a “warm room” and a genuine health tool.

Check the link in my bio to read the 20-year JAMA study on the benefits of heat exposure impacts cardiovascular health and longevity.

We spent the last month down in this basement in the Mt Tabor neighborhood. The home owner wanted to add an additional bedroom and make it a play area for the kids. It started as a pretty dark, unusable storage space, but we opened it up to be something functional and nearly doubled the usable space of the home. 

The 1200 sq ft was split into two rooms. One as a guest room. Another as the play area with two egress windows to bring in the light from the east facing walls. We trenched out inside the foundation to ensure that any water that comes in will get pumped out before it hurts the renovation. 

Material choices:

- Marmoleum floors: Great option for basements as it holds up to moisture well, is very resilient in high traffic areas and looks great.

- Cork floors: Cork is both a natural material from our mother, Earth. The home owners chose it for the play areas to create warmth and it’s slight give for your feet helps with those inevitable crashes by the kids :)

- Maple frame: We used solid maple for the window jambs without trim. It takes a little longer to do and requires precise cuts but it creates a beautiful clean look for decades.
